sec.title: Keymessage
sec.p: GBS read coverage analysis identified a Robertsonian chromosome from two Thinopyrum subgenomes in wheat, conferring leaf and stripe rust resistance, drought tolerance, and maintaining yield stability.

sec.title: Abstract
sec.p: Agropyron glael (GLAEL), a Thinopyrum intermedium × Th. ponticum hybrid, serves as a valuable genetic resource for wheat improvement. Despite its potential, limited knowledge of its chromosome structure and homoeologous relationships with hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum) has restricted the full exploitation of GLAEL's genetic diversity in breeding programs. Here, we present the development of a 44-chromosome wheat/GLAEL addition line (GLA7). Multicolor genomic in situ hybridization identified one chromosome arm from the St subgenome of Th. intermedium, while the other arm remained unclassified. Genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) read coverage analysis revealed a unique Robertsonian translocation between two distinct Thinopyrum subgenomes, identified as 4StS·1JvsS. The GLA7 line demonstrated strong adult plant resistance to both leaf rust and stripe rust under natural and artificial infection conditions. Automated phenotyping of shoot morphological parameters together with leaf relative water content and yield components showed that the GLA7 line exhibited elevated drought tolerance compared to parental wheat genotypes. Three years of field trials showed that GLA7 exhibits similar agronomic performance and yield components to the wheat parents. This unique addition line holds promise for enhancing wheat's tolerance to multiple stresses through the introduction of new resistance genes, as well as its ability to mitigate the effects of temporary water limitation during flowering, all without negatively impacting wheat performance.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is the most widely cultivated cereal globally, providing food for 40% of the world’s population and serving as the primary cereal crop in Europe, including Hungary. The development of high-yielding, stress-tolerant wheat cultivars with desirable quality traits is essential to address the challenges posed by global climate change. Rust diseases and abiotic stress factors, such as heat and drought, are the primary yield-limiting factors for wheat. It is projected that the frequency of rust epidemics and extreme heat and drought events will increase over the next 20 years due to climate change (Hansen et al. 2012). Leaf rust, caused by Puccinia triticina Eriks., is the most prevalent rust disease, significantly reducing the quality and productivity of wheat. The detrimental effects on wheat foliage include disruption of photosynthetic activity, dehydration, cell death, and premature defoliation, leading to reduced grain filling (Fatima et al. 2020). Yield losses in susceptible wheat cultivars may exceed 50%, though typical losses range from trace amounts to 30% (Wellings 2011). Currently, more than 80 leaf rust resistance genes have been formally cataloged in wheat (https://wheat.pw.usda.gov/GG3/wgc, McIntosh et al. 2020). Many of these genes have been sourced from wild species related to wheat, and several (e.g., Lr9, Lr19, Lr24, Lr25, Lr29, and Lr35) continue to offer effective protection against pathogen attacks in Central Europe (Vida et al. 2011). Until 2014, the predominant rust species affecting wheat in Hungary was Puccinia triticina. However, during the 2013/2014 growing season, Puccinia striiformis f.sp. tritici emerged as the dominant pathogen, posing a significant threat to wheat production, similar to trends observed in other European countries (Jevtić et al. 2020). This pathogen, responsible for stripe or yellow rust, can cause yield losses of up to 60%. Since 2014, it has consistently overwintered in Hungary, a trend linked to rising average winter temperatures. By 2023, pathotypes PstS7, PstS8, PstS10, and PstS13 were identified in Central Europe (Słowacki et al. 2024). Among these, PstS10 has been the most dominant since 2011, accounting for more than 80% of the isolates studied (Ali et al. 2014). As of now, 86 Yr genes (Yr1-Yr86) have been formally cataloged (McIntosh et al. 2020). Additionally, over 100 provisionally designated genes and more than 300 quantitative trait loci (QTL) associated with stripe rust resistance have been documented (Feng et al. 2023; Zhu et al. 2023). However, the continual evolution of pathogen populations necessitates the incorporation of new resistance gene alleles to maintain effective disease control.

Drought became a critical abiotic stress factor in agriculture, significantly limiting biomass production (Araus et al. 2002). It impedes the growth of stems and roots (Blum 1996), reduces the assimilating leaf area (Passioura 1988), decreases tiller number (Cone et al. 1995), and inflicts pollen sterility and ovule abortion, all contributing to notable yield losses. Drought occurring during the meiosis developmental stage has been identified as having a particularly severe impact on fertility and yield components (Barnabás et al. 2008). Therefore, breeding lines that exhibit tolerance to drought occurring at heading stage could play a crucial role in developing varieties with improved yield stability under water-limited conditions. One of the most significant challenges for breeders is to identify and utilize appropriate genetic variation within the wheat pangenome to enhance resistance against pests and diseases, as well as tolerance to extreme abiotic conditions, all while maintaining high-yield potential.

The genetic diversity of wheat can be significantly enhanced through interspecific hybridization by incorporating or substituting chromosomal segments from wild relatives. The use of wild relatives, landraces, and isolated breeding gene pools as plant genetic resources has played a crucial role in wheat breeding, contributing to increased tolerance to biotic and abiotic stresses and improving grain yield, nutritional value, and end-use quality (reviewed by King et al. 2024). Species within the genus Thinopyrum (Löve 1982; Dewey 1984) have been widely utilized as gene sources in various breeding programs (Wang 2011; Ceoloni et al. 2013). The two most prominent species within this genus are the hexaploid Thinopyrum intermedium (Host) Barkworth & D.R. Dewey (2n = 6x = 42, StJrJvs) and the decaploid Thinopyrum ponticum (Podp.) Barkworth & D.R. Dewey (2n = 10x = 70; JJJJsJs). These species are notable for their resilience to extreme environmental conditions such as low and high temperatures, drought, wind erosion, soil salinity, and nutrient imbalances (Friebe et al. 1996; Witcombe et al. 2008; Lu et al. 2022; Giovenali et al. 2023; Tounsi et al. 2024). Additionally, several rust resistance genes from these species have been successfully integrated into wheat through the transfer of chromosomal segments: Lr19 (Sharma and Knott 1966), Lr24 (McIntosh et al. 1977), Lr29 (Procunier et al. 1995; Friebe et al. 1996), Lr38 (Friebe et al. 1992, 1993), Sr24 (Sears 1973), Sr25 (McIntosh et al. 1977), Sr26 (Friebe et al. 1996), Sr43 (Kim et al. 1993), Sr44 (Friebe et al. 1996; Khan 2000), YrT14 (Guo et al. 2023), Yr50 (Liu et al. 2013), Yr69 (Hou et al. 2016), and YrL693 (Huang et al. 2014).

Tsitsin (1979) developed a 56-chromosome hybrid by crossing Th. intermedium (previously known as Agropyron glaucum) with Th. ponticum (formerly Agropyron elongatum) to combine the advantageous traits of these species. This hybrid was informally named Agropyron glael (hereafter GLAEL), reflecting an abbreviation of the parental species’ names. Both parent species possess complex genomes, but comparative analyses between Th. intermedium and wheat chromosomes have demonstrated macrosynteny between the 21 chromosomes of Th. intermedium and their homoeologous in the A, B, and D genomes of wheat (Cseh et al. 2019). In GLAEL, the genomes of two wheatgrass species were recombined, with chromosomal rearrangements being identified (Kruppa and Molnár-Láng 2016). Although some subgenomes can be discriminated, the homoeologous and syntenic relationships of the specific chromosomes with those of wheat remain unknown. In previous work, partial amphiploid lines resistant to leaf rust and stripe rust were developed through the wheat × GLAEL crossing program (Kruppa et al. 2016), and a 6Jvs·6D centric fusion line with enhanced tillering was identified (Türkösi et al. 2024). However, abiotic or biotic stress-tolerant addition, substitution, or translocation line carrying a chromosome (or segment) from this hybrid species had not been produced before.

The chromosome-mediated gene transfer to wheat relies on the ability to screen large pre-breeding populations for the presence of alien chromatin (King et al. 2018). Since GLAEL carries chromosomes from five different Thinopyrum subgenomes (Kruppa and Molnár-Láng 2016), precise identification of the foreign genome in the progeny lines can be challenging. The most advanced wet-laboratory techniques for the detection and characterization of introgressions are molecular cytogenetic methods like C-banding (Gill et al. 1991; Danilova et al. 2017), fluorescence- and genomic in situ hybridization (FISH, GISH, mcGISH, and ND-FISH) (Rayburn and Gill 1986; Schwarzacher et al. 1989; Mukai et al. 1993), and other wet-laboratory methods based on dot-blot genomic hybridization (Rey and Prieto 2017), acid or SDS-PAGE (Milovanović et al. 1998). These methods are complex, though, and are not suitable for screening large populations. PCR-based molecular marker techniques can also be utilized to identify Thinopyrum introgressions (Ko et al. 2002). For the detection, identification, and characterization of introgressions from Thinopyrum species, the combination of GISH, FISH, and molecular markers has become widespread in practice (Yu et al. 2019; Guo et al. 2023; Yang et al. 2023; Gong et al. 2024). However, the disadvantages of these methods are that they are still inaccurate for species with complex genomes, time-consuming, and limited in their ability to detect small foreign segments.

Genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS), utilizing restriction enzymes (restriction site-associated DNA (RAD-seq) and double-digest restriction site-associated DNA (ddRAD-seq)), was developed to reduce genome complexity and enhance targeted sequencing efforts (Elshire et al. 2011; Poland et al. 2012). GBS read coverage analysis is particularly effective in detecting both major and minor chromosome introgressions and deletions (Tikhenko et al. 2024). When aligned with a reference genome, this method can also identify the wheat homoeologous group that the introgression most closely resembles. The implementation of GBS for identifying wheat/Thinopyrum introgressions represents a significant leap forward. Advancements in next-generation sequencing have enabled genome-level examination of several wheatgrass species. Chromosome-level assemblies have been successfully completed for diploid Th. elongatum (Wang et al. 2020). GBS has played a crucial role in the genetic analysis of Th. intermedium. Kantarski et al. (2017) created the first consensus genetic map for Th. intermedium, consisting of 21 unclassified linkage groups (LGs) and demonstrating strong collinearity and synteny with Triticeae genomes. Wang et al. (2020) employed a mapping population of Pseudoroegneria spicata (an ancestor of Th. intermedium containing the St genome) and identified 3468 GBS markers, revealing 35% homology, 86% synteny, and 0.85 collinearity with the A, B, and D genomes. Their comparative analysis of GBS data between Ps. spicata and Th. intermedium suggested that Kantarski’s unclassified LGs 2, 4, 8, 11, 13, 17, and 21 correspond to the St genome. Using this approach, Qiao et al. (2021) aligned Th. intermedium GBS sequences with Th. elongatum (Wang et al. 2020). Their analysis concluded that Thi-LG 1, 6, 7, 10, 14, 18, and 20 could be assigned to the Je genome, while the remaining LGs were attributed to the Js genome. Recently, the reference genome assembly for Th. intermedium has been released (Th. intermedium v3.1 DOE-JGI, http://phytozome.jgi.doe.gov/). The final assembly contains 21 chromosomes, encompassing 99.992% of the assembled sequences, with their numbering and orientation determined by the subgenome groups J (Jr), S (St), and V (Jvs). The availability of these sequence data facilitates the precise identification of Thinopyrum chromosomes, including the chromosomes of GLAEL, thereby accelerating the discovery of new resistance genes, which remains a primary objective in the utilization of Thinopyrum species for breeding purposes.

This study reports on the production and comprehensive characterization of a wheat-Thinopyrum addition line that demonstrates robust resistance to leaf rust and stripe rust, along with substantial drought tolerance during the flowering stage. The objectives of this research were threefold: (1) to establish the chromosome number and detailed composition of the newly developed line using genomic and fluorescence in situ hybridization; (2) to investigate the structure of the incorporated Thinopyrum chromosome and its macrosynteny with wheat through read coverage analysis, utilizing GBS data from the double‐digest restriction site–associated DNA sequencing (ddRAD-seq) protocol and available reference genomes of hexaploid wheat cultivar Chinese Spring, Th. intermedium, and diploid Th. elongatum; and (3) to comprehensively evaluate the agronomic traits of the line, including its resistance to rust diseases through spontaneous and induced infections, the impact of drought stress on yield-determining parameters using an automated phenotyping platform, and the influence of the alien chromosomal segment on wheat agronomic performance under field conditions over two growing seasons and three locations.

sec.title: Plant materials
sec.p: Wheat genotype Mv9kr1 (hereafter MV9), containing both the recessive crossability alleles (kr1kr1kr2kr2) (Molnár-Láng et al. 1996), was crossed with GLAEL, a hybrid of Th. intermedium × Th. ponticum produced by Tsitsin (1979). The sterile F1 plants were maintained in tissue culture; regenerated plants were successfully backcrossed with Chinese Spring. The BC1 progenies were self-pollinated, resulting in several leaf rust and stripe rust resistant partial amphiploids with 56–58 chromosomes (Kruppa et al. 2016). The progeny lines were backcrossed with the rust susceptible Mv Karizma (hereafter KAR) elite wheat variety for 2 consecutive years to produce offspring with fewer chromosomes and phenotypic characteristics more similar to wheat (Fig. 1). An introgression line GLA7 was selected in the BC3F2 generation. For the detailed analysis of the selected line, specific DNA sequences were amplified from several related plant species: Th. bessarabicum (2n = 2x = 14, JbJb, USDA W610232), Ps. spicata (2n = 2x = 14, StSt, USDA D2836), Aegilops tauschii (2n = 2x = 14, DD, MvGB605), Secale cereale L.cv Ryefood (2n = 2x = 14, RR), and T. aestivum cv Mv9kr1 (2n = 6x = 42, BBAADD).

sec.title: Molecular cytogenetic analyses
sec.p: Germinating seedlings were grown on a hydroponic system. Root tip meristem cells were synchronized using hydroxyurea dissolved in Hoagland solution and accumulated in metaphase using amiprofos-methyl (Doležel et al. 1992; Vrána et al. 2016). Chromosome spreads were prepared using the air dry drop method (Kato et al. 2004). To detect Thinopyrum (GLAEL) chromatin within the wheat genetic background, the following genomic probes were employed during multicolor genomic in situ hybridization (mcGISH): genomic DNA from Ps. spicata (to detect the St genome), and genomic DNA from Th. bessarabicum (to detect the J genome). The probe was prepared using the BioPrime™ DNA Labeling System (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). For St genome labeling, a modified dNTP combination including digoxigenin-11-dUTP from Roche was utilized. The hybridization mixture contained 3000 ng of bread wheat DNA as a block and 100 ng of each labeled probes per slide, dissolved in a 15 μl mixture of 100% formamide, 20 × SSC, and 10% dextran-sulfate at a ratio of 5:1:4. Hybridization was performed overnight at 42 °C. During the detection phase, digoxigenin and biotin were visualized as red and green signals using anti-digoxigenin rhodamine Fab fragments (Roche, Basel, Switzerland) and streptavidin-Alexa Fluor 488 conjugate (Molecular Probes, Waltham, USA) dissolved in TNB (Tris-NaCl-blocking buffer).

Slides were analyzed using a fully automated high-throughput Zeiss Axio Imager Z2 upright epifluorescence microscope (Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany). Vectashield Antifade Mounting Medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories, Newark, USA) was used to preserve fluorescence. Images were captured with a MetaSystems CoolCube 4 USB Laboratory Camera and analyzed using Metafer 4 (automatic metaphase image capture) and ISIS (image processing) software (MetaSystems, Altlussheim, Germany).

After capturing mcGISH images under the microscope, the slides were washed three times for 30 min in 2 × SSC at 25 °C to remove the signals. The slides were then re-hybridized using FISH DNA probes Afa-family, pSc119.2, and oligo-pTa71. DNA repeats were amplified from the genomic DNA of Ae. tauschii and S. cereale using PCR (Nagaki et al. 1995; Contento et al. 2005). The BioNick™ Labeling System (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) was utilized for labeling the pSc119.2 and Afa-family probes; for the latter, a modified dNTP mixture including digoxigenin-11-dUTP from Roche (Basel, Switzerland) was used. Integrated DNA Technologies (Coralville, IA, USA) synthesized the oligonucleotide probe pTa71 (Tang et al. 2014). Digoxigenin and biotin were added to the synthetic oligonucleotides at their 5′ ends, and when combined in a 6:5 ratio, a yellow signal was detectable. The FISH protocol was modified as follows: The hybridization temperature was 37 °C for probes pSc119.2, Afa-family, and pTa71. The hybridization mixture (30 µL per slide) contained 20 ng of oligo-pTa71, 70 ng of each of the pSc119.2 and Afa-family probes, and salmon sperm DNA as a blocking agent. The slides and overlay signals from the FISH analysis were re-examined under the microscope.

sec.title: GBS library construction- ddRAD-Seq
sec.p: Genomic DNA was extracted from fresh young leaves of wheat donor genotypes MV9 and KAR, the parental Thinopyrum hybrid GLAEL, and the GLA7 line in 96 well plates using BioSprint DNA kit (Qiagen Inc.) following the manufacturer’s protocol. As the basis for double-digest restriction site-associated DNA (ddRAD) library protocol development, the protocol of Yang et al. (2016) with minor modification was followed: (1) restriction enzymes MspI and SphI were used; (2) the sequences of P1 and P2 adapters with barcodes and primers with indexes were designed according to Poland et al. (2012); (3) pooled samples were size-selected for fragment sizes of 350 to 390 bp using a dye-free Blue Pippin 1.5% gel cassette (BDF1510) (Sage Science, Beverly, MA, USA). All sublibraries were pooled equimolarly and sequenced on the NovaSeq 6000 platform (Illumina) using the SP reagent kit v.1.5 in 2 × 150 bp configuration at the Institute of Experimental Botany, Czech Academy of Sciences, Olomouc, Czechia.

sec.title: GBS read coverage analysis
sec.p: An “in silico wheat × Thinopyrum hybrid” was created by concatenating the reference sequences of a donor and a recipient species in order to create a reference assembly. For identification of wheat-GLAEL introgressions, we combined the Chinese Spring reference genome (IWGSC RefSeq v2.1) (Zhu et al. 2021) and Th. intermedium (as a parental species of GLAEL) draft genome assembly (Th. intermedium v3.1 DOE-JGI, http://phytozome.jgi.doe.gov/). An additional combined reference was generated using the Chinese Spring wheat reference and diploid Th. elongatum (Wang et al. 2020). When combining reference genomes, all chromosomes or pseudomolecule names were specified to be unique. Illumina short reads of the GLA7 addition line and its wheat (MV9 and KAR) and GLAEL parents as control were separately mapped to this mixed genome using HISAT2 v2.1.0 (Kim et al. 2019). Sequence alignment, normalization of the read counts, and data filtering were performed using a high-throughput bioinformatics pipeline following the protocol of Adhikari et al. (2022).

sec.title: Disease resistance tests
sec.p: Adult plant resistance (APR) to stripe rust (Puccinia striiformis f.sp. tritici, Pst) was evaluated in field-grown plants following natural infections during the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 seasons. According to Global Rust Reference Center for yellow rust (GRRC) (https://agro.au.dk/forskning/projekter/rustwatch/), the Amboise race, a new variant of PstS10 genetic group, occurred in this area in 2023. This race can only be distinguished by this variety, with virulence to yellow rust resistance genes Yr1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 17, 25, and 32, and avirulence to Yr5, 8, 10, 15, 24, and 27. Observations were recorded at the ‘Tükrös’ nursery (Martonvásár, Hungary, geographic coordinates: 47°18′40′′N 18°46′56′′E) in 2023, and in an experimental field specialized for rust inoculations (the ‘Rustgarden’, Martonvásár, Hungary, 47°19′05.7′′N 18°46′23.9′′E) in 2024. The susceptible wheat cultivars MV9 and KAR were planted adjacent to plots containing the MV9/GLAEL introgression lines. Rust symptoms were scored on the 0–9 scale described by McNeal et al. (1971) in which a score of 3 or less is considered highly resistant.

APR to leaf rust was tested for the GLA7 line, the wheat parents MV9 and KAR in the Rustgarden, providing natural isolation from other breeding nurseries during the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 growing seasons. Near-isogenic lines in the background of Thatcher with known Lr genes were included as references; Lr9 and Lr29 were effective against leaf rust in both seasons. To evaluate the APR of the tested genotypes, rows of a spreader variety (Alcedo) were planted around them and inoculated at Zadoks growth stages 37–39 (Zadoks et al. 1974) using a mixture of uredospores. The spore suspension was injected into the spreader plants with a hypodermic syringe, facilitating the natural spread of the pathogen from these primary infection sources. In May and June 2024, ideal meteorological conditions for the development of leaf rust symptoms led to a severe epidemic in the other two experimental fields ‘Tükrös’ and ‘Prebreed’ (Martonvásár, Hungary, clayey-chernozem, 47°19′39″N, 18°47′01″E). Consequently, leaf rust APR was evaluated across all three experimental field locations in 2024. The extent of infection at Zadoks growth stages 77–83 was assessed by measuring disease severity using the modified Cobb scale (Stubbs et al. 1986) and determining the host response, which was categorized as resistant, moderately resistant, intermediate, moderately susceptible, or susceptible.

sec.title: Phenotyping of drought tolerance
sec.p: The drought tolerance of GLA7 and the parental wheat genotypes (MV9 and KAR) were investigated using a PlantScreen™ modular high-throughput phenotyping system installed in Martonvásár by the Photon System Instruments Ltd. (PSI, Brno, Czech Republic). Germinated seeds were planted in Jiffy pellets, and 5 days later, they were vernalized at 4 °C for 6 weeks under low light intensity (20 µmol m −2 s −1). After vernalization, the plants were grown in 2L pots (1 plant/pot) filled with a 3:2:1 mixture of garden soil, compost, and sand and placed in 2 × 2 trays in complete randomized blocks design in a climate-controlled growth chamber (Walk-In FytoScope FS-WI, PSI, Brno, Czech Republic). Eight replicates were used for each genotype. Different growth protocols were used according to the plant’s developmental stages. Until tillering, the plants were grown under a day/night temperature of 15/10 °C under photoperiod of 12/12 h at a light intensity of 250 µmol m−2 s−1 composed of 30% cool white, 40% deep red, and 30% far-red. In booting period, the day/night temperature and photoperiod were increased to 17/12 °C and 14/10 h at 350 µmol m−2 s−1 light intensity. At flowering stage, the temperature was fixed at 19/16 °C under photoperiod of 16/8 h at 350 µmol m −2 s −1 light intensity, while the temperature was increased by 2 °C in grain filling period.

The drought treatment was started at the beginning of booting period (Zadoks 41, flag-leaf sheath extending) just before the start of flowering. The control plants were irrigated daily as before to keep the optimal water status of soil, while the drought stress was induced by withholding water for 10 days. Control and drought-treated plants were automatically phenotyped for morphological and physiological traits using the red–green–blue (RGB) sensors of the PlantScreen™ platform before and after drought treatment, as described by Awlia et al. (2016). The data and images were analyzed by PlantScreen™ software tool package according to the software instructions (PSI, Brno, Checz Republic). Plant-specific pixel data from the RGB images were classified and the relative percent of different color categories were shown as color segmentation data. After high-throughput measurements, flag-leaf segments were collected to determine relative water content (RWC), according to Darkó et al. (2020). After flowering, the normal water status of plants was restored, and the plants were growing till ripening. At harvest, the shoot weight and grain parameters (grain weight, length, and width) were determined. Seed length, seed width (mm), and thousand grain weight (TGW) were measured using a MARVIN 5.0 Seed Analyzer (MARViTECH, Wittenburg, Germany).

sec.title: Field phenotyping experiments
sec.p: The GLA7 addition line and the parental wheat genotypes (MV9 and KAR) were sown by hand in the pesticide-free nursery ‘Tükrös’ during the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 growing seasons. Sixty grains of each genotype were sown in 6 × 1 m rows, with 10 grains per row and a row spacing of 0.15 m. Ten plants from each genotype were randomly selected for analysis. In the 2023–2024 season, these genotypes were also sown at two additional locations. In the ’Pre-breeding’ and in the ‘Rustgarden' experimental field, 300 grains of each genotype were sown in 2 m2 plots (6 × 2 m rows; 50 grains per row) with a row spacing of 0.15 m. Experimental plots were sown using a HEGE-80 plot drill, and harvesting was conducted manually. When necessary, artificial fertilizers, herbicides, and insecticides were applied, but fungicides were not used. To minimize the confounding effects of soil and microclimatic variables, genotypes were seeded in close proximity. Plant height and tillering (spikes per plant) were measured in the field immediately before harvest. Post-harvest measurements included the length of the main spike (cm), the number of spikelets per main spike, the number of seeds per main spike, the number of seeds per spikelet, and the number of seeds per plant. Seed length and width (mm) were measured using a MARVIN 5.0 Seed Analyzer (MARViTECH, Wittenburg, Germany). Thousand grain weight (g) was also calculated. Additionally, the timing of heading was recorded according to Tottman (1987).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Significant differences between the GLA7 line and the wheat genotypes MV9 and KAR were determined using Tukey’s post hoc test in IBM SPSS Statistics 20.0 software (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). This analysis was performed on data from 10 biological replicates for each year and field nursery. For the indoor phenotyping of drought tolerance, significant differences among the three genotypes and treatments were calculated from eight biological replicates, employing the same statistical methods as described for the field trials.

sec.title: Molecular cytogenetic analyses
sec.p: Chromosome constitution of the GLA7 BC3F2 line was analyzed using mcGISH. Genomic DNA of Ps. spicata (St) and Th. bessarabicum (Jb) was utilized as functional DNA probes for the genome-wide identification of Thinopyrum chromosome. An introgression line with 44 chromosomes was identified. A St genome chromosome arm (a subgenome of Th.intermedium) was indicated by a strong red fluorescence signal, while the absence of green hybridization signals suggested no involvement of J-genomic fragments in the addition line. The genomic origin of the other arm of the added chromosome remains unclear due to a very faint St signal (Fig. 2a).

sec.p: Following the mcGISH procedure, the signals were captured under the microscope, then sequentially removed. The slides were subsequently subjected to FISH analysis using repetitive DNA probes Afa-family (red), pSc119.2 (green), and oligo-pTa71 (yellow) to determine the FISH karyotype of the added chromosome and identify the wheat chromosomes. The GISH results were consistent with the previously reported FISH patterns for bread wheat chromosomes, confirming the presence of every individual A, B, and D chromosome with no observed rearrangements or deletions among the wheat chromosomes. Afa-family (red) signals were detected on the subtelomeric region of the long arm of the introgressed chromosome (Fig. 2b). This FISH pattern did not entirely correspond to any known wheat chromosome patterns (Fig. 2c), suggesting that it might represent a Thinopyrum arm from a third genome that is unmarked by the St or Jb genomic probes and is most definitely not wheat.

sec.title: GBS read coverage analysis
sec.p: We applied GBS technology to identify potential chromosomal deletions and rearrangements, as well as to determine the homoeologous relationship of the added Thinopyrum chromosome to wheat. The quality filtered read data from MV9, KAR, GLAEL, and GLA7 genotypes were aligned to the combined T. aestivum-Th. intermedium (T.a.-Th.i.) reference genomes. The GBS read coverage analysis identified the structure of whole GLAEL chromosome in the GLA7. In line with the molecular cytogenetic analysis, GBS read data identified the presence of 4St short arm together with the short arm of 1 Jvs in GLA7 addition line.

In detail, the average read count on the ABD reference genome for GLA7 was comparable to those of MV9 and KAR wheat parents, confirming the presence of all wheat chromosomes in the addition line (Table 1, Fig. 3a). However, only 101.8 reads per Mb were detected on chromosome 1B, compared to 181.1 and 231.1 reads per Mb in the wheat controls, and nearly half of the counts observed on other B chromosomes suggesting the presence of only one copy of 1B in the sequenced line. The normalized read counts of GLA7 along the in silico hybrid enabled a more comprehensive analysis, revealing both the number and density of reads across individual chromosomes simultaneously (Fig. 3b). In two instances, the GLA7 read density along the J (Jr), S (St), and V (Jvs) in silico chromosomes deviated significantly. Specifically, along the first 175 Mb of the 4S in silico chromosome, a consistent density of 126 reads per Mb was detected, indicating an introgression from the 4St short chromosome arm into the wheat background (marked by turquoise—color arrow in Fig. 3a, b). This chromosome arm was also detected by mcGISH. In contrast, only 2.0 reads per Mb were observed along the remainder of the 4S in silico chromosome (176–377 Mb) showing the absence of this chromosome region in GLA7. Additionally, 134 reads per Mb were identified along the first 255 Mb of the 1V in silico chromosome, proving the presence of an introgression from the 1Jvs short arm (marked by purple—color arrow in Fig. 3a, b). Whereas only three reads per Mb were present in the remaining portion of the 1V in silico chromosome, indicating the absence of this chromosome region in GLA7 addition line. These findings indicate another major introgression from the GLAEL parent into wheat which was not detectable by mcGISH. St genomic GISH probe had a faint hybridization signal on the telomeric region of this chromosome arm. In summary, the GBS read coverage analysis revealed the presence of all wheat chromosomes, and Thinopyrum introgressions derived from short arm of 4St and 1Jvs chromosomes in the GLA7 addition line.

sec.p: Significant details about the parent lines were also revealed by the GBS read coverage analysis. When the MV9 and KAR wheat control genotypes were aligned to the combined T. aestivum-Th. intermedium (T.a.-Th.i.) reference genome, 174–309 reads per Mb bin along the 21 wheat chromosomes, and only 0.1–4.5 reads per Mb along the 21 wheatgrass in silico chromosomes were detected (Table 1, Fig. 3a). This indicated the presence of all wheat chromosomes in both MV9 and KAR, although a small deletion was evincible on chromosome 2D of MV9 between the 575 and 622 Mb bins (Online Resource Fig. S1a), which was absent in KAR and GLA7. The lowest read per Mb was observed on chromosome 1A in MV9, with 173.9 reads per Mb, while the highest was on chromosome 7D, with 309.1 reads per Mb in the case of KAR. The wheat parental genotypes exhibited consistent read coverage across the Chinese Spring wheat reference genome.

When GLAEL was mapped to the combined reference genome, low read counts (1.8–12.1 reads per Mb) were observed on wheat in silico chromosomes, indicating the absence of the ABD genome. However, the D genome showed almost four times more reads per Mb than the A and B genomes. The number of GLAEL reads per Mb on the S, J, and V in silico chromosomes averaged 77.8, 94.9, and 57.7, respectively, with the highest sequence match to the J genome and the lowest to the V genome. Significant variations in read density were observed across different chromosomes, with a two to threefold increase in read counts per Mb in certain chromosome regions, as clearly illustrated in the normalized read count plot (Online Resource Fig. S1b). The pattern of read coverage plots is unique for chromosomes 7S, 2V, 3V, and 4V, where the coverage values change suddenly from 0–1 to 4–5 in the centromeric/pericentromeric regions (i.e., read counts per Mb increase by 2 to 3 times), suggesting that these chromosomal regions possess additional copies.

Given that GLAEL is not solely derived from Th. intermedium but also includes Th. ponticum as a parental species, we aimed to utilize another genome in our analysis that might be more similar to Th. ponticum. Sequence data for Th. elongatum were considered as an alternative. Therefore, the analysis was extended by using a wheat-Th. elongatum (T.a.-Th.e.) in silico hybrid. For the MV9 and KAR, we obtained the same read values as on the T.a.-Th.i. hybrid (Online Resource Fig. S2). The number of GLAEL reads /Mb on the in silico hybrid A, B, D, and E chromosomes averaged 5.1, 4.1, 30.2, and 72.3, respectively, with the D genome having 6–7 times higher read alignment compared to the A and B genomes. GLA7 has only 2.7 reads/Mb reads on in silico E chromosomes, with no outstanding values in the read density. There was no introgression from the Thinopyrum E genome into the wheat in GLA7.

sec.title: Disease resistance observations
sec.p: During a severe stripe rust epidemic in May 2023, observations revealed that the adult MV9 and KAR wheat genotypes were susceptible to the Pst race, exhibiting infection types (ITs) of 8 and 6, respectively. In contrast, plants carrying the Thinopyrum chromosome displayed high resistance, with an IT of 0 (Fig. 4a). The epidemic led to an average yield loss of 24% among the Martonvásári (Mv) wheat varieties in 2023. Leaf rust also appeared on the leaf surfaces that remained intact following the yellow rust outbreak, with GLA7 remaining symptom-free (some plants showed a trace (T) level of infection, characterized by very small, isolated pustules affecting less than 1% of the leaf area). Both wheat parents were moderately susceptible, with ITs of 20MS (moderately susceptible, covering about 20% of the leaf area) and 40MS recorded for MV9 and KAR, respectively.

sec.p: In 2024, the stripe rust epidemic was less severe, but infection types 5, 7, and 0 were still recorded for the MV9, KAR, and GLA7 genotypes, respectively. Additionally, in 2024, alongside artificial infection in the Rustgarden, a spontaneous leaf rust epidemic occurred in the other two nurseries, where 60S for MV9, 20MS for KAR, and 0R for GLA7 were observed (Fig. 4b). Artificial leaf rust resistance tests in 2024 further evaluated the infection response of the GLA7 addition line (Fig. 4c). The parental wheat genotype MV9 and the KAR variety were severely infected, with ITs of 100S and 40MS, respectively, while the addition line showed immunity (0%), with some plants exhibiting a hypersensitive reaction (HR).

sec.title: Drought tolerance
sec.p: Gamete formation, involving meiosis and subsequent mitotic cell divisions (Zadoks 39–41), represents one of the most sensitive developmental stages of wheat for drought stress, which strongly affects the yield. At this stage, withholding watering for 10 days caused a more pronounced effect on leaf senescence in the case of wheat genotypes MV9 and KAR than in GLA7 (Fig. 5a). Due to the chlorophyll degradation, this symptom can be followed by plant phenotyping through color segmentation with the use of RGB sensors. At the end of drought treatment, the shoot of wheat parents exhibited higher percent of yellow parts (Fig. 5b) and a more intense decrease in their total shoot area relative to GLA7 (Fig. 5c). Parallel with these visible symptoms, the decrease in RWC was much more pronounced (30–40%) in the drought stressed wheat Mv9 and KAR than in GLA7, where only a slight RWC decrease (~ 10%) was observed (Fig. 5d).

The relative percent of different colors are shown. c–i Mean values of plant area (dm2), relative water content (RWC, %), shoot weight (g), grain weight per plant (g), thousand grain weight (TGW, g), grain length (mm), and grain width (mm) for each genotype. Standard errors of the means are represented as error bars. Two-way ANOVAs with Tukey’s post hoc tests were performed for all tested genotypes for each yield parameter separately under control and drought stress treatments (α = 0.05, n = 8). Different letters above error bars indicate statistically significant differences among treatments as determined by Tukey’s post hoc tests

sec.p: The symptoms of drought stress have also been manifested at maturity, with the shoot weight per plant significantly lower (~ 18% and ~ 15%, respectively) in drought-treated Mv9 and KAR compared to their untreated control. In contrast, no significant decrease in shoot biomass (3.4%) was detected in GLA7 (Fig. 5e). The applied drought treatment had a more pronounced effect on the fertility-related yield component, grain weight per plant (Fig. 5f), with Mv9 and GLA7 showing 31.8% and 36% decreases, respectively, while the elite wheat cultivar KAR exhibited a drastic 85% decline. The 10-day drought treatment also caused a 42% and 47.7% decrease in the thousand grain weight (TGW) of the wheat parental lines (Mv9 and KAR), despite restoring the soil water content to the optimal level in the remaining plant development stages (booting, inflorescence development, anthesis, milk development, dough development, and ripening) (Fig. 5g). On the other hand, no significant drought-induced decrease in TGW were detected in GLA7. Interestingly, parallel with the decrease in TGW, wheat lines exhibited a more intense (18.2%, 13.1%) decrease in grain width (Fig. 5i) than grain length (3.5%, 7.3%) (Fig. 5h). In the case of GLA7, only grain length showed a 2.7% decrease, while no significant changes were detected for grain width.

sec.title: Field phenotyping experiments
sec.p: The agrometeorological parameters of the 2 years studied were similar. From sowing to harvest, the growing sites received 430 mm (2022–2023) and 460 mm (2023–2024) of rainfall, with 105 mm and 120 mm falling during the grain filling phase. The number of heat days with temperatures exceeding 30 °C was 5 in 2023 and 7 in 2024 until harvesting. Based on these data, the years are well comparable. The plants of the GLA7 addition line did not differ from wheat controls in terms of most of the examined parameters. Its plant height in the 2024 Rustgarden nursery is significantly greater, with no significant differences observed at other locations (Table 2). It ranges from 86 to 98 cm, with each plant producing 5–7 spikes. Spike length was the longest for the addition line at all locations, but only in Tükrös in 2024, it showed a significant difference compared to both wheat controls. The approximately 12 cm long, loose, awnless spikes contained 21–24 spikelets, with an average of 2.2–3.0 grains per spikelet (Fig. 4d). The tillering of the addition line was significantly lower in 2023, but in 2024, it was similar to that of the wheat parents.

sec.p: No significant differences were observed compared to the wheat parent varieties in terms of the number of spikelets per spike, number of grains per spikelet, and number of grains per plant. The most notable differences were observed in grain size parameters and thousand grain weight across both years and locations. The grain width and length as well as thousand grain weight were generally lower than those of wheat controls. In 2023, the flowering time coincides with that of wheat controls; while in 2024, flowering began approximately 10–15 days earlier due to prolonged warm spring temperatures.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Wheat genetic resources have great potential to decrease environmental footprints, prevent disease pandemics, and increase food security (King et al. 2024). In the face of rapidly evolving wheat pathogens exacerbated by climate change, there is an increasing need to enhance breeding processes for greater efficiency.

In the past, the detection and identification of Thinopyrum segments in wheat relied on molecular cytogenetic methods. However, introgressed segments smaller than 30 Mb were often undetectable in wheat (Gao et al. 2021). Consequently, the presence of foreign chromosome segments frequently went unnoticed as cryptic introgressions, with their existence inferred only by the manifestation of resistance traits in the background of susceptible wheat (Yingshan et al. 2004; Liu et al. 2013; Zhan et al. 2014). In this study, only one Thinopyrum St genome chromosome arm was detected in wheat background using mcGISH, while the other arm of the alien chromosome displayed a faint signal. The phenomenon that the Jb genome of Th. bessarabicum does not hybridize to the all J genome of Th. intermedium during GISH has already occurred several times. Cseh et al. (2019) found that the Jb genomic probe did not hybridize to the 14 chromosome of Th. intermedium and only revealed the 14 Jr chromosomes. At the same time, the St genomic probe produced a dispersed red signal over the telomeric regions of all 14 Jvs chromosomes, as it happened in our case. Türkösi et al. (2024) were likewise compelled to use molecular markers during the identification of the 6D·6Jvs centric fusion, as unlabeled Thinopyrum chromosome parts stayed after a detailed molecular cytogenetic analysis. Identifying such unmarked segments can often be achieved by labeling and utilizing a third species, Dasypyrum villosum (Mahelka et al. 2011; Cseh et al. 2019). This faint signal could also indicate cross-hybridization with the wheat D genome, as Thinopyrum species are more closely related to the D genome than to the A and B genomes (Liu et al. 2007; Cseh et al. 2019). Our results indicate that GLAEL produced 4–7 times more reads on the wheat D genome in silico chromosomes compared to the A and B genome chromosomes, suggesting a close relationship between the Thinopyrum genomes and the D genome.

GBS has emerged as a robust method for genomics-assisted breeding across a range of species, including those with complex genomes. The two-enzyme ddRAD-Seq approach offers suitable and uniform complexity reduction (Poland et al. 2012), producing high-quality polymorphism data at a relatively low-cost per sample. The initial results of using GBS techniques for the identification of introgressions have been published over the past decade, supporting the breeding of various economically important crops such as rice (Arbelaez et al. 2015), barley (Hoseinzadeh et al. 2020), cotton (Adhikari et al. 2023), and wheat (Keilwagen et al. 2023). The first GBS analysis for wheat-Thinopyrum introgressions was published by Adhikari et al. (2022). In the present study, GBS read coverage analysis clarified the deficiencies left after the molecular cytogenetic analyses, as unambiguously indicated the presence of a 255-Mb 1Jvs Thinopyrum chromosome segment (arm) and a 175 Mb 4St chromosome segment (arm), ruling out the presence of any additional wheat arms beyond the complete 42-chromosome wheat genome. Assuming that both chromosome arms broke at the centromere and fused, their segment sizes (175 Mb of 377 Mb for 4St, and 255 Mb of 573 Mb for 1Jvs) indicated that both arms are short arms. Based on these findings, it is clearly established that the foreign chromosome in the GLA7 addition line is a 4StS·1JvsS Robertsonian translocation, with the St arm being shorter, as corroborated by the cytological measurements of the chromosome. Centric fusions between wheat and Thinopyrum have been frequently documented, including examples such as T7BS·7S#3L (Liu et al. 2011), T2EbS·2BL (Ghazali et al. 2015), T1AS·1EL (Tanaka et al. 2017), and 6DS·6Jvs (Türkösi et al. 2024). Centric fusions between wheat and Thinopyrum have been also found by Grewal et al. (2018), who reported non-homoeologous J genome chromosomes having Robertsonian translocations such as DA1JS·6JL. Additionally, there have been reports of Robertsonian chromosomes formed between two distinct Thinopyrum subgenomes, such as 5JsS·3StS and 5Js·3StS, as described by Yu et al. (2019).

Beyond identifying the Thinopyrum chromosome arms, the analysis also revealed significant information about the parent lines. In the MV9 genotype, a deletion was detected between the 575–622 Mb region of chromosome 2D when compared to the Chinese Spring reference genome; this deletion was absent in the KAR and GLA7 genotypes. Independent studies have reported the presence of wheat yellow mosaic virus (WYMV) resistance genes/QTLs on 2DL in various wheat cultivars, all of which are located within the same genetic region (Liu et al. 2005; Nishio et al. 2010; Kojima et al. 2015; Suzuki et al. 2015; Xiao et al. 2016). Chen et al. (2023) further refined the mapping of QTL QYm.nau-2D to the 596.0–614.8 Mb interval on chromosome 2D of Chinese Spring, identifying it as an exotic introgression from the N genome of Aegilops uniaristata. In this study, we identified the deletion of this region in MV9, indicating the absence of this WYMV resistance QTL, while the presence of the N-genomic fragment was not confirmed by read coverage analysis using the Nv genome assembly of Ae. ventricosa (Liu et al. 2024) as reference (data not shown) in the KAR and GLA7 genotypes.

In the case of the GLAEL parent, the read coverage analysis to the S, J, and V in silico wheatgrass chromosomes revealed significant variations in read density within individual chromosomes. According to Adhikari et al. (2022), this type of analysis is capable of assessing chromosomal dosage in aneuploidy, allowing for the straightforward differentiation of zero, one, or two copies. A distinctive GBS profile was observed in GLAEL. Significant variations in read density were noted across chromosomes, with a two to threefold increase in read counts per Mb in specific regions, as clearly illustrated in the normalized read count plots. This can be attributed, in part, to the presence of Th. ponticum in the GLAEL, as some of its chromosomal segments are likely to align with those of Th. intermedium, given their close genetic relationship. Previously several minor Jr-St and Jvs-St translocations were observed in GLAEL (Kruppa and Molnár-Láng 2016), likely occurring during the formation of the artificial hybrid. As a result, GLAEL contains a unique chromosome composition where the five different genomes from the parental species have recombined. Additionally, the exceptional genetic diversity within wheatgrass species could result in varying outcomes depending on the accession analyzed. Thus, for wheatgrasses with complex genomes, it is unlikely to observe a near-uniform GBS read coverage profile with consistent density and read values, as seen in wheat. It is precisely this valuable trait—genetic diversity—that has driven the incorporation of these species into wheat breeding programs.

Numerous wheat/Thinopyrum introgression lines with rust resistance have been published but few involve homoeologous groups 1 or 4. Notable genes identified include Sr24, Lr24, and YrE on homoeologous group 3; Sr26 and SrB on homoeologous group 6; and multiple genes on homoeologous group 7 such as Lr19, Lr29, Sr25, Sr43, Sr44, and Yr14. Yr69 is located on homoeologous group 2. Yr50, derived from Th. intermedium, was mapped to wheat chromosome arm 4BL, but the presence of a small Thinopyrum chromosome segment was not detectable with GISH (Liu et al. 2013). Wang et al. (2020) reported the first stripe rust and powdery mildew resistance linked to chromosome 1Js originating from Th. ponticum. The 1Js chromosome substituted the 1B and carried powdery mildew and leaf rust resistance according to Li et al. (2021). Recently, Yr1EL (Wu et al. 2024) and Yr4EL (Gong et al. 2024) stripe rust resistance genes from tetraploid Th. elongatum were identified and transferred into common wheat via T1BS⋅1EL and T4DS·4EL translocation lines, respectively. Additionally, Zheng et al. (2020) transferred the resistance gene YrCH-1BS from Th. intermedium to hexaploid wheat. The leaf rust and stripe rust resistance genes cataloged so far have not been identified on the 1Jvs and 4St arms, indicating that the resistance genes carried by GLA7 differ from these known genes. This is supported by leaf rust tests, which showed that among the controls, near-isogenic lines containing the Lr29 and Lr9 genes were resistant. However, Lr9 is not derived from Thinopyrum, and Lr29 has been identified on the homoeologous group 7 chromosome, rather than chromosomes 1 or 4. Due to GLAEL's unique hybrid nature, resulting from extensive recombination between the two parental species, the resistance genes it harbors may differ from those present in the parent species. This makes the utilization of this resistant line particularly valuable.

The value of this line is further emphasized by the results from the drought tolerance experiment conducted at the most critical developmental stages, which have a substantial impact on yield. The findings demonstrated that both KAR and MV9 were significantly more sensitive to a 10-day water deficit compared to the GLA7 line. Based on previously published research, the Thinopyrum parent lines of GLA exhibit multiple tolerance to drought and salt stress through complex mechanisms. Th. ponticum can survive under high drought and salt conditions, possibly due to its strong root system, higher root/shoot ratio, relatively complete antioxidant enzyme system, Na+ accumulation, and stable K+/Na+ ratio in roots (Zhang et al. 2022). Maintaining the chlorophyll concentration and the photosynthetic capacity of the leaves is key adaptive trait under water-limited conditions and plays a crucial role in determining crops drought tolerance (Chernyad’ev and Monakhova 2003). Drought tolerance involves the maintenance of high chlorophyll content to support the plant's photosynthetic capacity under stress (Yasmeen et al. 2013). Shafqat et al. (2019) examined wheat-Th. bessarabicum chromosome 1J–7J addition lines under 15% PEG-induced stress and revealed that disomic addition lines 1J, 2J, and 4J demonstrated minimal reductions in chlorophyll a content, underscoring the significance of these chromosomes in conferring drought tolerance. The results for chlorophyll b indicated that addition lines 1J, 4J, 7J exhibited minimal reduction. Our results on GLA7 addition line, which contains the short arms from chromosome group 1 and 4 (as a centric fusion 4StS·1JvsS), showing that the green leaf area was not reduced during the drought stress, are in line with previous findings. The GLA7 line showed promising tolerance to drought stress applied before flowering, with a stable green leaf area and no adverse effects on the yield components tested. Although the molecular mechanisms underlying drought tolerance were not the focus of this study, a more detailed investigation is currently underway.

By integrating the chromosome arms into the wheat genome during breeding while preserving their beneficial traits, the typical yield-reducing effects often associated with introgression lines are not expected. Production of wheat/Thinopyrum recombinants is necessary for effective inclusion in breeding programs. For this purpose, we have already initiated crosses with the Mv9kr1 ph1b mutant (Türkösi et al. 2022), and the selection and identification of recombinants are expected soon. Molecular cytogenetics techniques used before have not been as good at finding Thinopyrum introgressions as GBS read coverage analysis, which is supported by available Thinopyrum sequence data. Reducing the need for fungicides to manage rust diseases can primarily be achieved through the identification and incorporation of new disease-resistant genes into cultivars. For this purpose, the newly developed wheat/Thinopyrum introgression line, which has shown adult plant resistance, is an excellent resource.
